strengths: The paper provides a clean, unified mathematical framework (Φ-normalized attention) that covers softmax, linear, focused, and differential attention, and gives a correct (if simple) dispersion theorem with proofs in the appendix; Table 1 usefully summarizes dispersion bounds across attention variants.

The theoretical dispersion analysis is well motivated and connects to recent literature ([29], [11], [12], [32]), correctly pointing out that differential attention is still Θ(1/n) and relating the dispersion rate to the choice of ϕ.

SEMA is a simple, explainable design (window softmax attention + homogeneous averaging) that is directly motivated by the theory, and it achieves competitive results: 83.7 top-1 on ImageNet-1K at 26M params, better ImageNet scaling at 384²/672²/768² than VMamba-T with fewer FLOPs, and strong COCO Mask R-CNN 3x results.
An ablation study (Table 5) isolates the contribution of the averaging term, and the limitations section is honest about the asymptotic nature of the theory, untight bounds, and constrained compute.

Reproducibility is reasonably supported: training hyperparameters, computing resources, and the full architecture (Table 6, Fig. 4) are provided, and one baseline (MILA-T) was retrained from the authors' source code.
weaknesses: The core theoretical contribution is incremental: the main theorem is essentially an extension of Theorem 2.2 in Velicković et al. [29] (the paper admits this), and the proof reduces to a boundedness-of-logits argument plus a trivial min/max bound. The theorem's practical relevance is limited because the interesting regime is finite n, where the bounds (ϕ(a)/(nϕ(b)), ϕ(b)/(nϕ(a))) are loose and do not explain the observed finite-scale behavior.

The central design jump is heuristic: 'attention disperses as n→∞' does not by itself justify that arithmetic averaging is the right global component; a mean-pooled global branch is a very old, generic idea (reminiscent of global average pooling tokens / PoolFormer-style mixing), and the paper does not compare SEMA against a simple Swin window-attention + global-average baseline to show the specific combination is meaningfully better.

Novelty relative to MILA [13] is narrow: SEMA largely retains the MILA macro-architecture and swaps linear attention for window softmax attention plus averaging; the 'Mamba-like' framing is loose, and the connection to Mamba's exponential forgetting is argued only qualitatively.

Empirical margins are small and fragile: the headline gain over MILA-T is 0.2% top-1 (the same as the averaging ablation alone, likely within seed-to-seed variance, and no error bars or multiple seeds are reported); the COCO 1x results are not consistently best-2 despite the text's claim.

Despite 'Efficient' in the title, no wall-clock throughput or memory measurements are reported—only FLOPs—so efficiency claims are not directly validated; only tiny (~26-30M) models are evaluated, with no larger scale experiments due to compute limits.

Restricted experimental scope: hyperparameter tuning is minimal (e.g., only a couple of window sizes for COCO), no language modeling or long-context experiments where the dispersion theory would be most relevant, and no public code release is stated, which weakens reproducibility of the full pipeline.

Presentation has notable sloppiness: Equation (3)'s argument for the unbounded case is sketchy, 'casual' for 'causal' and other typos appear, RoPE is applied to Vw in Algorithm 1 (likely an error), and the Table 1 differential-attention bounds deserve more careful justification given possible negative coefficients.

strengths: The paper is generally well-organized and clearly written, unifying softmax attention, linear attention, focused attention, MILA, and differential attention in a single Φ-normalized framework (Definition 3.3, Table 1), which aids readability and comparison.

The dispersion analysis (Lemma 3.2, Theorem 3.4) is correct under its stated assumptions and provides a simple, coherent motivation for a local-plus-global design, and the authors honestly discuss when the boundedness assumption fails (Remark 3.5).

The proposed SEMA module is simple, efficient, and easy to implement (window attention plus broadcast averaging of V), and the evaluation covers ImageNet-1K classification, higher-resolution fine-tuning (384²–768²), and COCO Mask R-CNN, comparing against a reasonable set of recent baselines.
The limitations section is candid about the gap between the asymptotic theory and finite n, untight bounds, and restricted compute/model sizes.
weaknesses: Limited originality of the theoretical contribution: the central dispersion result is an adaptation of Theorem 2.2 of Velicković et al. [29] (as the authors themselves acknowledge), and the proof is a direct consequence of bounded logits under any continuous normalization; several observed cases (softmax, linear, focused, MILA) follow mechanically from the same one-line bound, so the theory mainly repackages known phenomena.

The theory-to-design link is weak. The claim that softmax(qK^T)V ≈ (1/n)Σ v_j in the large-n regime is not actually justified: the Θ(1/n) bound involves the constant ϕ(b)/ϕ(a), which can be exponentially large in logit magnitude, so no uniform approximation error is controlled. The averaging term is better characterized as a heuristic low-pass mixing than a theoretically consistent approximation of full attention.

Empirical gains are marginal and possibly within noise: +0.2% top-1 over MILA-T on ImageNet-1K, while SEMA has more parameters (26M vs 25M) and FLOPs (4.3G vs 4.2G); the ablation (Table 5) shows the entire contribution of the averaging component is exactly 0.2%, meaning SEMA without averaging already matches MILA-T. No variance/seeds or significance analysis is reported.

The scalability claim ('outperforming recent vision Mamba models on increasingly larger scales') is over-stated relative to evidence: Table 3 compares only against VMamba-T, omitting MILA and other Mamba-like baselines at higher resolutions, and only tiny (~30M) models are evaluated despite scalability being the headline claim.

The dispersion motivation stems from long-context behavior, yet no sequence-length or language-modeling experiments are provided that would empirically validate the theory or show SEMA retains attention sharpness as n grows; there is also no empirical measurement of dispersion coefficients to corroborate Table 1.

Ablations are minimal: only the averaging term is ablated. No ablation over window size (the COCO result with window 12 hints it matters), value projection, RoPE placement, or comparisons against alternative global-mixing mechanisms (e.g., pooled-token attention, grafting, pooling operators used in prior efficient vision models), which are closely related to simply averaging V.

Some typos and sloppiness undermine confidence: learning rate reported as 4×10^3 (presumably 4×10^-3), 'casual' for 'causal', garbled equation fragments (e.g., Eq. 10), and the sentence claiming SEMA 'outperforms' models with which it merely ties at 83.5.

Reproducibility concerns: no code release is mentioned, key implementation details (e.g., exact RoPE/LePE integration, value projection) are only partially described, and the reported gains depend on reproducing MILA's training recipe exactly.

strengths: The paper provides a unifying formalization (Definition 3.3) of softmax, linear, focused, and differential attention under one Φ-normalized framework, and derives dispersion bounds (Table 1) that cleanly explain and compare known empirical observations from prior work (e.g., [11], [29], [32]).

The design of SEMA is simple, clearly specified (Alg. 1, Alg. 2, Eq. 13), and directly motivated by the theoretical analysis; the connection between Mamba's exponential forgetting and window attention is a nice conceptual framing.

Empirical evaluation is reasonably broad for the compute available: ImageNet-1K at 224², finetuning at 384²/672²/768² demonstrating scalability, and COCO instance segmentation under standard 1x/3x Mask R-CNN protocols, with comparisons against well-matched baselines (VMamba-T, MILA-T, CSWin-T, etc.).

The limitations section is honest and specific (asymptotic vs. finite n, non-tight bounds, limited downstream tasks, no hyperparameter tuning), and an ablation study (Table 5) isolates the contribution of the averaging term.
Experimental details (training recipe, batch sizes, hardware, architecture specification in Table 6) are thorough enough to support reproduction.
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is thin: Theorem 3.4 is a direct generalization of Theorem 2.2 of Velickovic et al. [29] (the authors say so themselves), and Lemma 3.2 follows immediately from continuity on a compact set. The bounded-logits assumption needed for Lemma 3.2 is strong, and the theorem becomes vacuous if ϕ approaches zero on the domain, which is not discussed.

There is a logical gap between the theory and the method: the theory shows attention disperses as n → ∞, but SEMA operates at n ≈ 196–3136 where dispersion is far from the asymptotic regime. The claim that 'softmax(qKᵀ)V ≈ (1/n)Σvⱼ' in the useful regime is asserted, not demonstrated; no empirical measurement of actual attention entropy/dispersion at the scales used is provided to validate that the motivating phenomenon occurs in practice.

The empirical gains over the closest baseline are marginal: SEMA achieves 83.7 vs. 83.5 for MILA-T, and the ablation shows the averaging term—the paper's core novel component—contributes only 0.2%. No variance over random seeds is reported, so it is unclear whether the improvements are statistically meaningful.

Limited novelty of the architecture: window attention plus a global token-mixing operation (here, value averaging) closely resembles established designs (Swin plus pooling-based mixers, MetaFormer/PoolFormer-style global mixing, FocalNet-style local-global combinations), and the macro-architecture is taken directly from MILA. The delta over MILA-T is essentially replacing linear attention with window softmax attention plus averaging.

Scale of validation is narrow given the claims: only ~26–30M parameter 'tiny' models are trained (the scalability claim rests on finetuning, not pretraining, at larger resolutions), and no language or long-context experiments are included despite dispersion being fundamentally a long-context phenomenon.

Reproducibility is weakened by the absence of any code release statement, and some experimental choices are under-justified (e.g., only a couple of window sizes tried for COCO, window size 12 chosen without systematic study).

Presentation issues: Table 1's differential attention lower bound can be negative while the stated range is a subset of [0,1]; Eq. (3)'s counterexample uses unbounded logit growth in a way that deserves more careful discussion; several typos ('casual' for 'causal', Eq. 9 notation) and Figure 1/2 are referenced loosely relative to the algorithms.

strengths: The paper provides a unifying formalization of softmax, linear, focused, window, MILA, and differential attention under a generalized Φ-normalized attention framework, and proves a dispersion result (Theorem 3.3) plus a probabilistic variant (Proposition 3.5) with proofs in the appendix; the dispersion analysis is meaningfully connected to recent empirical observations (Velickovic et al. 2025; Han et al. 2023/2024).

The proposed SEMA design (window attention + a global arithmetic average of values) is simple, well-motivated by the asymptotic analysis, easy to implement (Algorithm 1), and preserves the Mamba-like macro-architecture, making it a drop-in replacement for MILA.

Empirical evaluation is reasonably broad: ImageNet-1K at three model scales (83.7/84.6/85.4 top-1, slightly above MILA), COCO Mask R-CNN, ADE20K segmentation, runtime comparisons showing 10-33% speedup over MILA at large resolutions, and a valuable scaling study up to 2048² resolution where SEMA degrades more gracefully than VMamba (64.7 vs 57.4 at 1024² before finetuning).

The ablations are informative and honestly reveal that at 224² the averaging term contributes little (+0.2%) while at higher resolutions its contribution grows (+2.2% no-tune at 672²), which is consistent with the dispersion theory; the limitations section (Appendix A) candidly discusses the asymptotic nature of the theory and limited hyperparameter tuning.
Reproducibility support is adequate: architecture details (Tab. 10), training hyperparameters, computing resources, and source code in supplemental materials are provided.
weaknesses: The central theoretical result is close to trivial: bounded logits on a compact domain imply attention coefficients are O(1/n). While correctly proven, this is a fairly direct observation already substantially anticipated by Velickovic et al. (2025) (whose dispersion-coefficient analysis the authors themselves acknowledge subsumes their bound as a special case), limiting the originality of the theoretical contribution.

The proposed method is architecturally very simple — Swin-style window attention plus a fixed, input-independent mean of the value vectors — and the link between this 'homogeneous mixing' and the dispersion theory is loose: the averaging term is a constant additive vector, not a consequence derived from the asymptotic analysis, and the paper provides no direct evidence that dispersion is the phenomenon the averaging actually corrects.

The practical gains are modest and partly confounded: at the standard 224² resolution the improvement over MILA appears largely attributable to the added value projection (ablation: +0.8%) rather than the averaging mechanism that gives the paper its name, and at late stages window size 7 equals the full 7×7 feature map, so 'window attention' is effectively full attention there; the headline scaling benefits rest on a resolution regime with few baselines (only VMamba) and single-run results.

Some claims are under-supported: the assertion that MILA's actual implementation 'is not causal' and hence disperses is asserted briefly with details in an appendix; the probabilistic proposition's covariance-sparsity condition (≤ n^α pairs, α<2) is a strong and somewhat arbitrary assumption whose plausibility for real attention scores is not verified empirically.

Scope is limited to vision; no language or long-sequence results are provided despite the dispersion phenomenon being arguably most relevant in that regime, and citation hygiene issues exist (e.g., a '2026' textbook citation for Vershynin's 2018 book, and reliance on a concurrent 'Dayag et al., 2026' work for medical results rather than original experiments).

strengths: The paper provides a clean, unified formulation (Φ-normalized attention) that covers softmax, linear, focused, window, MILA, and differential attention, and uses it to give a compact statement of the dispersion phenomenon (Theorem 3.3, Proposition 3.5), which is pedagogically useful.

The proposed method (SEMA) is simple, well-motivated within the paper's framework, and easy to implement (Algorithm 1); the accompanying ablations (Tables 7-8) honestly isolate the contribution of the averaging term versus the value projection.

Evaluation spans multiple standard benchmarks (ImageNet-1K, higher-resolution generalization, COCO, ADE20K) and includes runtime comparisons against the closest baseline MILA, showing favorable scaling behavior at large resolutions (Table 4).
The limitations section (Appendix A) candidly acknowledges that the asymptotic theory may not bind at practical token counts, that bounds are not tight, and that hyperparameter tuning was limited.
Experimental settings, architecture details (Table 10), and computing resources are documented, and source code is stated to be included in supplementary materials.
weaknesses: Limited originality of the theoretical contribution: the core dispersion result (Theorem 3.3) is essentially a compactness/boundedness argument that formalizes and restates the dispersion phenomenon already established in Veličković et al. (2025); the paper itself concedes its 'Theorem 2.2 is a special case' style relationship. Proposition 3.5 is a routine application of Chebyshev's inequality to covariance-bounded variables.

A logical tension in the motivation: the theory shows full attention disperses and window attention avoids dispersion, yet the proposed 'global' component is precisely the dispersed (averaging) limit. The paper embraces dispersion rather than avoiding it, which undercuts the causal chain from the theorem to the design; the justification for why adding a raw mean of values is the right global approximation is largely hand-wavy.

Empirical gains are marginal at the standard operating point: at 224² SEMA-T improves over MILA-T by only ~0.4 top-1 (83.7 vs 83.3), and the ablation attributes only +0.2 to the averaging component at that resolution. The headline 'scalability' advantage over VMamba (Table 3) is largest in the no-tuning regime (+2.2 at 672²) but shrinks to +0.4 after fine-tuning.

Fairness concerns in the higher-resolution comparison: SEMA is fine-tuned for 30 epochs while VMamba baselines use 10 epochs with a different (whole-network vs linear) finetuning protocol, making the central 'robustness at scale' claims hard to attribute to the method rather than the protocol.

Single-run results are reported for most experiments, with no variance or significance testing, which is problematic given sub-point differences are used to claim superiority; the authors note tuning was constrained, limiting the strength of SOTA comparisons.

Citation integrity issues: several references appear future-dated or hard to verify (e.g., 'Dayag et al., 2026' for USEMA, 'Vershynin, 2026'), and Table 9 in Appendix C reports third-party results from the 2026 USEMA paper rather than experiments run by the authors, weakening evidential support for the medical-imaging generality claims.

Downstream results (COCO Table 5, ADE20K Table 6) are competitive but not clearly superior, with 'bold best-2' framing obscuring that SEMA trails VMamba-T in several metrics (e.g., mIoU 48.2 vs 47.9 SS is a small margin, and MS is worse).

The practical relevance of the asymptotic theory to the vision setting is thin: the paper's own dispersion-rate estimates suggest dispersion arises at much smaller token counts in language than vision, yet no language experiments are provided, leaving the framework's generality asserted rather than demonstrated.

strengths: The paper offers a clean, unifying formulation (Φ-normalized attention) that covers softmax, linear, focused, window, MILA, and differential attention, and Table 1's summary of dispersion bounds per variant is genuinely useful for organizing the literature on attention 'dispersion'.

The theoretical analysis is correct as far as presented: Theorem 3.3's compactness-plus-bounded-logits argument is sound (proof in Appendix B), and the probabilistic restatement (Prop. 3.5 via a covariance-bounded weak law) is a reasonable alternative perspective.

The empirical evaluation is broad and mostly well-executed: ImageNet-1K at three model scales, high-resolution generalization (Table 3), COCO instance segmentation, ADE20K segmentation, runtime comparisons (Table 4), and ablations (Tables 7-8). SEMA consistently outperforms its closest baseline MILA, and the high-resolution robustness result (e.g., 64.7% vs 57.4% at 1024² without tuning; better finetuned results at all resolutions) is a concrete, useful finding.

The paper is honest about limitations (asymptotic results vs finite n, no extensive hyperparameter tuning, single-run results, vision-only scope), which increases trust in the reported numbers, and source code is included in the supplement.
The method is simple and deployable: window attention plus an O(1) averaging term, giving measurable speedups over MILA (33% at 1024²) while improving accuracy.
weaknesses: The central theory is mathematically straightforward. Theorem 3.3 reduces to the observation that continuous functions on compact sets are bounded, hence softmax weights are Θ(1/n). The practical force of the result is limited: the bound M_h can be enormous, making N(h, ε) astronomically large, and the paper does not demonstrate that the theory predicts behavior at realistic token counts (n ≈ 3136–65536) beyond reporting empirical dispersion rates borrowed from prior work (Veličković et al., 2025).

The claim that 'any global attention mechanism inevitably disperses' is overreaching. The result hinges on bounded logits with n; mechanisms that scale logit magnitudes with n (e.g., adaptive temperature, learnable per-token scaling) are not covered, and the extension to differential attention is argued heuristically, not proven.

Novelty of the method is modest. Window (local) attention combined with a global average of values is a long-standing local–global hybrid idea (e.g., long-short range attention, AddOn-style global features, and average-token/global-token designs in efficient transformers). The paper does not compare against the natural simple baseline of window attention plus a learned global token or learned weighted average, so it is unclear whether the specific 'homogeneous mixing' is better than standard alternatives.

The ablations partially undercut the theoretical motivation: at the standard 224² resolution the averaging component contributes only ~0.2% (Table 7), and the paper itself explains that early-stage windows make window attention nearly full attention there. The dispersion-motivated averaging only matters at large resolutions and in the external medical results (Table 9, from a separate 2026 preprint). The theory-to-practice link is therefore weaker than the framing suggests.

Some experimental rigor issues: results are single runs; SEMA-B is evaluated on fewer downstream settings; the high-resolution comparison in Table 3 uses only VMamba-T as a competitor; finetuning protocols differ between SEMA (30 epochs, whole network) and VMamba (10 epochs), which complicates the robustness comparison; and hyperparameter tuning was constrained by resources.

Presentation/citation issues: references to Vershynin (2026) and Dayag et al. (2026) are future-dated/preprint citations relied on for key claims (Chebyshev inequality, medical validation of homogeneous mixing); the notation around Φ, ψ, and κ is heavy for the simplicity of the results; and Equation 2's '6/π²' style example is illustrative rather than load-bearing.
Reproducibility is reasonable (code, architecture table, hyperparameters) but the admission of no thorough tuning and single-run reporting means exact numbers may not be reliably reproducible.
